newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tax bill gives breaks to parents, investors.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tax bill gives breaks to parents, investors.

text.p: Congress will vote on a $94 billion net tax cut package this week that gives breaks to parents and investors, while raising costs for smokers and international airline passengers.
Tax cuts have been a top priority for Republicans and the package would be the first major American tax reduction in 16 years. Democrats also joined in to voice support for the bill.
Congressional Republican leaders and White House officials reached agreement on the details late Monday.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said the tax cuts did not threaten to derail efforts to lower the budget deficit.
"We can afford it in the shorter run and it is not going to undo the very real progress we've made in deficit reduction in the longer run," he said.
Lawmakers were optimistic that the tax bill would pass, with House and Senate votes expected Thursday.
House Majority Leader Richard Armey, Republican of Texas, said he did not expect any opposition to the bill from House Republicans.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said the majority of Democrats were likely to support it.
The biggest piece was a tax credit of $500 for each child under age 17, which would be a revenue loss to the government of about $85 billion over five years.

Education tax breaks amounted to about $40 billion over five years and would provide up to a $1,500 tax credit for the first two years of college costs and a 20 percent deduction of up to $5,000 in tuition for the second two years.
A cut in the top rate of the capital gains tax to 20 percent from 28 percent on investment profits would actually raise money for the government in the first five years, a congressional aide said.
That was due to an expectation that the rate cut would prompt some investors sitting on profits to sell and so more people would be paying taxes on their gains.
Over 10 years, however, the capital gains provisions would cause a revenue loss of about $20.1 billion, a senior congressional aide said.
A tobacco tax increase of 10 cents per pack in 2000 and 5 cents per pack in 2002 to 39 cents from the current 24 cents would raise $5.2 billion over five years.

That tax increase was to be attached to the spending bill. This would allow lawmakers from tobacco growing states to vote for the tax cut legislation but against the spending bill containing the cigarette tax increase.

Airline passengers would be tapped for an additional $3 billion in taxes over five years. By lowering an existing ticket tax and imposing a new passenger tax and international arrival and departure fees, total taxes would be boosted to $33 billion from $30 billion through the year 2002.
One group criticised Clinton's support of the tax cut.

"This is the kind of tax plan congressional Republicans have been proposing and the president has been attacking all year," Michael Ettlinger, tax policy director for Citizens for Tax Justice, said. "It's shocking that he appears to have agreed to it."
